newsitem.title: UAE: FEATURE-Gulf sheikhdom waits for oil bonanza.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Gulf sheikhdom waits for oil bonanza.

text.p: The Arab emirate of Ras al-Khaimah is the flip side of the oil revolution that transformed the Gulf from a virtual backwater to one of the West's enduring strategic and economic concerns.
But current high oil prices and new American investment may just be the trick to turn its fortunes around.
Ras al-Khaimah, perched just below the entrance to the waterway, is tantalizingly close to billions of barrels of oil trapped below the Gulf's ocean floor and desert sands.
Yet being close is light-years in the oil game, even if you are one of the seven sheikhdoms that make up the United Arab Emirates (UAE) which has the world's fifth largest reserves.
Ras al-Khaimah, smaller than Rhode Island with a population of just over 150,000, has struggled to find petroleum since 1938 but geology, geography and history have dealt it a raw hand.

Nature has decided not to offer up the deluge of petrodollars which transformed the UAE's dominant emirate Abu Dhabi and neighbouring Saudi Arabia, preferring instead water and rocks that form the backbone of its agriculture and quarrying economy.

But its fortunes may be set to change with the resumption of exploration drilling early next year by an American private firm which has Bahamas-based top U.S. investor Michael Dingman and former White House Chief of Staff John Sununu on its board.
"With regard to the future of hydrocarbon potential we are optimistic," said Felix Molloy, general manager of the Ras al-Khaimah Oil and Gas Co Ltd (RAK Oil and Gas).
The firm will complete an analysis of offshore and onshore seisimic data by the end of this year and from this will decide to drill two exploration wells in the first quarter of 1997.
RAK Oil and Gas has completed a 370 km (230 mile) high resolution survey of the emirate's onshore and is reassessing offshore data obtained by another explorer.

New drilling will be welcomed by the emirate's ruler who saw an all too brief gas and condensate spurt from the offshore Saleh in the late 1980s and then a near exodus of the remaining foreign energy firms who found just dry holes.
Output at Saleh of light oil known as condensate peaked at just 10,000 barrels per day (bpd), minor in contrast to UAE output of 2.2 million bpd and Riyadh's eight million.
Even getting oil from Saleh took drillers to a depth of 15,000 feet (4,500 metres), the deepest of any of the producing oil and gas fields of UAE members Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah.
"Its hydrocarbon potential now seems to be almost zero," the industry's Arab Petroleum Research Center announced last year.
Though few in the emirate expect major new finds in Ras al-Khaimah, the Dingman-backed firm could awaken interest in this and other plays in the region which have been neglected.
U.S. firm ARCO already has rights to the emirate's offshore Baih field and is looking at plans to resume production, an industry source in the UAE said.
The key though, other than geology, will remain the international oil price which determines profitability.
Oil prices have surged over recent months to their highest level since the 1991 Gulf War, climbing to more than $22 a barrel for Dubai export crude, compared with $16 in 1995.
